paragraphs: Friend, look at the two people in this chapter. Esther walks into a room where she could be put to death, and she doesn't rush. She has fasted, she has stood in the court, and when the king offers her up to half the kingdom, she asks for a banquet and then waits one more day (Esther 5:3-8). I think that's a woman who is not in a hurry to grab the moment, and the lesson for you is that waiting well is not the same as doing nothing.

Now look at Haman. He's got wealth, sons, and a promotion, and the text says it plainly: "Yet none of this satisfies me as long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate" (Esther 5:13). Friend, that is a man with a full cookie jar who is staring at the one empty spot. When pride and rage run the kitchen, no amount of dough is enough, and the advice he gets only feeds the fire, because Zeresh and his friends tell him to build the gallows and he is pleased (Esther 5:14).

So here's the big idea, baker. Every one of us is going to walk past a Mordecai who won't bow, and we get to choose what to do with that heat. Haman builds something to destroy a man, and I think that should make us look hard at what we are building with our anger and who we let advise us. The story isn't over, friend, and it is a long way from done.
